Accommodation Advice for
International Students in Vietnam
Finding a comfortable and stable place to live is one of the most important steps as you settle into life in
Vietnam. Whether you're staying short-term or looking for a long-term home, it's essential to understand
how renting works here — from contacting real estate agents to ending a lease.

Step 1: Looking & applying for rental property.

metadata.title: Accommodation Advice International Students Rmit

documents.content:
.

Step 1: Looking & applying for rental property.
Finding a place to live in Vietnam usually involves working with a real estate agent — a third-party who
helps connect you with available apartments or shared homes. Most agents speak basic English and are
familiar with working with international students.
Where to Search
You can begin your search through:
• RMIT’s Accommodation Suggestion List – trusted and student-friendly options

metadata.title: Accommodation Advice International Students Rmit

documents.content:
estion List – trusted and student-friendly options
• Google – search terms like “Apartment for rent in District 7” or “Studio near RMIT”
• Facebook Groups – look for expat or housing communities (e.g., “Apartments for Rent in
HCMC”)
How to Contact Real Estate Agents
Once you find a listing or agency:
• Clearly explain your budget, preferred location (e.g., District 7), length of stay, and
any specific requirements (furnished/unfurnished; utilities included, etc.)

metadata.title: Accommodation Advice International Students Rmit

documents.content:
(furnished/unfurnished; utilities included, etc.)
• Ask whether the agent charges any service fees or commission (some do, some don’t)
• Request photos or videos of the property if you can't visit in person
💡💡Pro tip: Most agents will use mobile apps like Zalo, WhatsApp
When You’re Ready to Apply
If you find a place you like:

## Page 2

2

• Schedule a viewing – either in-person or via video call if you're not in Vietnam yet. We
encourage you to visit the property in person.

metadata.title: Accommodation Advice International Students Rmit

documents.content:
We
encourage you to visit the property in person.
• Check the property’s condition, location, nearby amenities, and ask about utility costs.
• Review the lease agreement carefully — ask for lease in both English & Vietnamese.
• Be ready to provide:
o 📄📄 A copy of your passport
o 📄📄 Your student visa
o 📄📄 Your student ID (or Letter of Offer if not enrolled yet)

Step 2: Rental Contract (leases)
A contract is an agreement between you and the rental provider about what each of you will do, or

metadata.title: Accommodation Advice International Students Rmit

documents.content:
rental provider about what each of you will do, or
not do, while you are renting the property.
Lease Duration
• The standard lease in Vietnam is usually 6–12 months
• However, it is possible to negotiate a shorter lease (e.g., 3–4 months), especially if you're
staying for a short study period
💡💡Pro tip: Be upfront about your stay duration when talking to agents or landlords
What to Look for in the Contract
Before signing anything, ensure the contract clearly includes:

metadata.title: Accommodation Advice International Students Rmit

documents.content:
ng anything, ensure the contract clearly includes:
• Rental price (monthly rent amount and due date)
• Lease duration (start and end dates)
• Security deposit terms (how much, and move-out conditions under what conditions it will
be refunded)
• Maintenance responsibilities (what you fix vs. what the landlord handles)
• Utilities (what’s included in the rent, and what’s not)
• Early termination clause (Notice period for ending the contract (often 30 days))

documents.content:
nding the contract (often 30 days))

• Guest policy, pet policy, quiet hours, and any other house rules
• Make sure to clearly ask your landlord for resident registration with local police:
“Will you help me register my residence with the ward police?”
💡💡Pro tip: Ask agent/ landlord for a bilingual contract – It’s best to request a contract in both English
and Vietnamese.
Deposit & Advance Payment
Once the contract is agreed upon, you’ll typically be asked to pay:

metadata.title: Accommodation Advice International Students Rmit

documents.content:
is agreed upon, you’ll typically be asked to pay:
• A security deposit of 1–2 months' rent (varies by property and lease length)
• Sometimes 1 month’s rent in advance as a commitment
• Make sure to get a written receipt for all payments — this is important for your records and
for when you move out
💡💡Pro tip: Don’t hand over money unless you’ve reviewed and signed the contract.

Residence Registration – Don’t Skip This Step!

Residence Registration – Don’t Skip This Step!
All international students must have their residence registered with the local ward police. Failure to
register can cause issues with visa renewals or legal paperwork — so double-check that this step is
completed after you move in.
Usually, landlords or building management will handle this process for you. But do not assume it’s done
— always confirm and follow up.
They will typically need:
• A copy of valid passport & visa

metadata.title: Accommodation Advice International Students Rmit

documents.content:
typically need:
• A copy of valid passport & visa
• Your rental contract
Ask for signed confirmation by landlord once the registration is approved by local authorization.

Step 4: Ending Tenancy
To properly end your lease:

metadata.title: Accommodation Advice International Students Rmit

documents.content:
Step 4: Ending Tenancy
To properly end your lease:
• Notify your landlord in advance (usually 30 days’ notice is required but check your contract for
agreed term)
• Clean the property and repair any damage
• Return all keys and access cards
• Be present for a final inspection
• Ensure all utility bills are paid
• Your deposit will be refunded, minus any damage or unpaid costs
💡💡Pro tip: Living in Shared Housing - Sharing with others is a cost-effective option but requires good
communication.

metadata.title: Accommodation Advice International Students Rmit

communication.
• Discuss house rules, bills, rent, and cleaning schedules, guests, and quiet hours
• Ensure everyone’s name is on the lease, or that there's a written agreement with the head
tenant
• Be mindful of cultural differences and personal space

### RMIT Vietnam continues long-term commitment to talent development with its record 2026 Scholarship program worth more than 200 billion VND.

RMIT University Vietnam has announced the opening of its 2026 Scholarship program, offering 174 scholarships in research and merit-based categories with a total value of more than 200 billion VND.

hD Scholarship, which follow their own timelines.

ch more than triples the annual scholarship fund.

and transportation, infrastructure and logistics.

# Newbie 101: Unlock Library Power

### RMIT Library can feel intimidating at first with rows of books and unfamiliar systems you’re not quite sure about. But beyond being a place to study, RMIT library is one of the most powerful academic tools you can use to navigate your academic journey, both online and on campus.

metadata.title: Newbie 101: Unlock Library Power

documents.content:
your academic journey, both online and on campus.

More than bookshelves and silent floors, RMIT Library gives you access to academic databases, study spaces, research support, and tools designed to make assignments easier and less time-consuming. Learning how to use these resources early can save you hours of stress and help you feel more confident throughout the semester.

## Research your assignment with reliable sources from RMIT Vietnam Library

metadata.title: Newbie 101: Unlock Library Power

documents.content:
t with reliable sources from RMIT Vietnam Library

One of the biggest mistakes new students make while researching is relying on Google and Wikipedia. However, finding reliable academic sources among countless search results can be time-consuming and overwhelming.

As one of the largest English language libraries in Vietnam , RMIT Vietnam library gives you access to over 700,000 books, peer-reviewed journals, and course readings that your lecturers expect you to reference in assignments.

metadata.title: Newbie 101: Unlock Library Power

documents.content:
lecturers expect you to reference in assignments. For research papers and reports in particular, the library also provides access to specialised databases such as Euromonitor (Passport), Statista, and WARC, which offer credible up-to-date industry data and reports that can help you gain higher marks in the Research and Referencing rubric.

To get the most out of these tools, start with LibrarySearch , which works like a smarter search engine built for academic research.

metadata.title: Newbie 101: Unlock Library Power

documents.content:
marter search engine built for academic research. If you’re getting too many or too few results, use Advanced Search to refine your focus by keywords, titles, or language and find relevant sources more efficiently. You can also expand your results by searching through RMIT Library Australia for additional academic resources.

## Reference with confidence with RMIT Vietnam Library

Strong academic work requires accurate referencing and an understanding of copyright to use materials ethically.

metadata.title: Newbie 101: Unlock Library Power

standing of copyright to use materials ethically. When you’re unsure how to cite the RMIT Harvard style, which type of sources to cite, or if the Easy Cite guide still feels confusing, just ask the experts - our librarians, who know their books and citations inside out.

You can book a face-to-face consultation, drop by the consultation desk, or simply chat online for quick advice.

metadata.title: Newbie 101: Unlock Library Power

ion desk, or simply chat online for quick advice.

## Counselling and Psychological Services (CAPS)

RMIT Counselling and Psychological Services (CAPS) offer free, confidential, short-term counselling for all enrolled students. In-person and online sessions are available at Saigon South and Hanoi campuses, along with workshops and online resources to support your mental health and wellbeing. For longer-term counselling and mental health support, we provide referral assistance to appropriate external counselling and health providers.

## Equitable Learning and Accessibility

The Equitable Learning and Accessibility team (ELA) offers compassionate, inclusive support for students with disabilities, health conditions or caregiving roles. We’re here to help you build independence and achieve academic success at RMIT.

### We support students who

- Are neurodivergent (including Autism or ADHD)

- Have physical, sensory or mobility access needs (including with vision and hearing)

- Experience learning, neurological or communication differences

- Live with mental health concerns or long-term medical conditions

- Care for a family member or dependent with ongoing support needs

#### Personalised support

Meet with us to discuss your needs and create an Equitable Learning Plan (ELP): a plan shared with your teaching staff to help ensure you receive support in assessments and learning activities.

You’ll need to provide medical documentation to register with ELA. Don’t worry if you don’t have it yet, we can help you understand what’s needed and how to get it.

## Safer Community

Safer Community is here to help create a respectful, inclusive, and safe environment for all RMIT students and staff. We provide confidential support and guidance if you’ve experienced or witnessed concerning, threatening, or inappropriate conduct.

Safer Community advisors are experienced and trained to support students and staff who feel unsafe, harassed, threatened, or discriminated against.
